newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SingTel under pressure after second float.
newsitem.headline: SingTel under pressure after second float.

text.p: Singapore Telecommunications Ltd (SingTel) shares came under pressure on Tuesday, but analysts said there should be support for what has become a core holding for some fund managers.
The selling came as trading began of the latest tranche of shares sold by the government to Singaporeans.

"When the government first announced the second tranche offer of SingTel shares there was concern that the amount released would result in an overhang in the market, and now that concern has increased," said David Leow, investment analyst with stockbrokers Kay Hian Pte ltd.

Government invesment arm Temasek Holdings announced on Monday it was issuing 804 million shares at a discounted price of Singapore $2.50 (US$1.77) each to 1.53 million Singaporeans in the second tranche.
Another five million shares were issued to self-help groups.
Most Singaporeans were allocated between 500 to 700 shares each, and some rushed out to unload them for a quick profit when trading of the second tranche shares started on Tuesday.

SingTel shares were the most active on the Singapore bourse, with about 15.7 million changing hands. SingTel 100 (traded in board lots of 100 shares) ended at S$3.18, down 12 cents, while SingTel (traded in board lots of 1,000 shares) ended at S$3.22, down eight cents.
Leow said SingTel shares should see some fundamental support at around S$2.80 to S$3.00 as the telecom company is a core holding for fund managers who want Singapore exposure.
SingTel was included in the Morgan Stanley Capital Index (MSCI), a benchmark widely used by fund managers, in June.
"But technically, there is no support until S$2.50, which is the price of the discount shares," added Leow.
Timothy Wong, research manager with Vickers Ballas, said he expected S$3 to show good support.

"I don't think there will be that many sellers, though potentially there are a lot. If you look at the volume today, it is hardly a mass exodus considering more than 800 million shares were issued," said Wong.
But he added that fundamentally the stock was not cheap, trading at around 29 times 1997 earnings, and could see some downside from current levels.
ING Barings investment analyst David Toh was more bearish.
"I don't think the price will hold at S$3," he said. "It will probably go back to around S$2.70, which was where it was earlier this year before the stock was included in the MSCI.
